"Streets of Fury" proves that the Brawler genre never gets old if only there are enough new ideas put into it. Using digitized actors for player and enemy characters might not be new, thinking of "Mortal Kombat", but it is so well done here that its a completely new experience. "Streets of Fury" is ...

+ fluent animations - and here are lots of it, because ...
+ every character has multiple attacks, combos, and more that are a pleasure to see
+ classic urban feeling with nice backgrounds and some storytelling
+ unlockable characters and modes that really keep me motivated to continue

There is a limitation in using digitized actors, and that's the impossibility to integrate weapons (I guess, it would be possible, but its even more effort than already put into the animations). Too, the usual "throw the badguy" feature is missing, and there is little to no interaction with the scenery. But "Streets of Fury" nevertheless is worth a look, or two, or three.

Streets of Fury EX is a Beat'Em Up game, and an improved version of the old Streets of Fury game.

Play alone or with friends locally, using the myriad of characters, moves and furies to destroy your enemies.

[h2] Pros: [/h2]

- There's a lot of content. 26 different characters, 109 different supers, an insane amount of moves per character compared to most Beat'Em Ups. 

2 Campaigns, along a Custom mode allowing you to change the game in different ways. 2 PvP modes, a Survival mode, multiple Challenges, and a Tag mode that allows you to bring 2 characters and swap between them at any time. 

It feels like a Beat'Em Up sandbox. You can waste hours on Training mode alone discovering what each character is capable of.

- The music is great. There's a decent variety in the soundtrack, and most of them can play on Training mode, so you won't get bored while beating up the training dummy.

[h2] Cons: [/h2]

- No online co-op, this really screws with harder difficulties, which is designed on having multiple players.

- Bad game design. 

You can get hit during some cutscenes if you move too far, or even softlock the game if you hit an enemy during it.

The camera sucks, it's too zoomed in and it has a mind of its own. This leads to moments where enemies already begin their attack animation off-screen, or just straight up hit you off-screen.

New enemies constantly spawn out of nowhere with no warning.

Enemies have colored variants that do different things, but it's impossible to tell them apart in the middle of the chaos.

It's hard to tell in which lane enemies are, and being in the lane closest to the background makes it hard to see where you are if there's enemies nearby in other lanes. I wish enemies in other lanes became transparent when they're not in the same lane as you.

Way too many enemies have super armor for no reason.

Playing this game on the hardest difficulty is a nightmare. It throws in way too many enemies at once, even causing lag due to some areas having over 20 enemies simultaneously. Half of the characters don't have great crowd control, so they feel horrible to play in there.

Some enemies can freeze the player, this should be removed entirely. This allows players to be comboed for an insane amount of time. There was a time where my character's dead body was being juggled for [b] 40 SECONDS [/b] and there was nothing I could do about it. I could not respawn until they dropped the combo.

- The Plan A campaign has really bad sections: 14- Hip Hop Hideout, 15- Hip Hop Beating, 17- Eiffel Tower.

14: A single lane with problematic enemies that constantly spawn out of nowhere. Just add another lane to this section.

15: Boss that can freeze you. Just remove the freeze.

17: Spam enemies that can freeze you. Again, just remove the dumb freeze.

- And then, we have the worst thing in this game. The second campaign: Plan B

Instead of just defeating the gang leaders, you try to make them join you instead. This is not a bad idea on paper, however, the first 2 allies you get are horrible.

You probably heard the phrase "Better than nothing", right? It genuinely would be better if these 2 dudes weren't here.

Jay C. Binkman, the first one, sucks. He takes forever to start shooting. And if you try to juggle or air combo nearby, you can't because he will shoot that enemy, launching them far away from you with his gun.

And then we have MC Manhattan, the worst travesty in this game. The main gimmick of this character is his dropkick, he does it in almost all cutscenes, and the playable version has 5 different dropkicks. The sound he makes when he dropkicks is used for the level up, and is even reused for Max's dropkick in Streets of Rage 4. So guess what the ally version never does? The dropkick. What he does instead is a garbage kick that launches the enemy, preventing you from doing ground combos if you're near him.

So now we have the deadly combination of clown that prevents you from doing juggles and bozo that prevents you from doing ground combos. Surely it can't get worse than that right?

Ladies and gentleman, I present to you, the worst section I have ever played in a Beat'Em Up: Stage 6- Tough Negotiations. 

This area introduces the Truck enemy, an enemy that hits the ground, creating a explosion. This enemy is problematic on its own, massive hitbox, super armor, and he breaks your guard if you try to block.

This already sounds bad enough, but for some reason this area spams that enemy. You will constantly get hit by him from off-screen due to your stupid allies triggering his attacks.

The attack can be avoided by jumping... until the game spawn enemies that anti-air you... peak game design right here.

You also need to fight a boss before you get into this section, and you don't get healed after defeating him.

This area is the worst part of the game and [b] needs [/b] to be changed. Make it so there can only be 1 Truck at a time. Dude is a walking hazard, it should never have more than 1. I don't care if you have to buff him to compensate, just make so the player doesn't have to deal with multiples of the guy.

And this isn't the only poorly designed enemy, stage 11- That Guy is Dinamyte, introduces a kamikaze enemy, and they also suck.

They have too much armor and way too much health. The best strategy is to just let your allies activate their explosions so you don't have to deal with them.

He needs to be reworked. Make it so he now has less stamina and only 1 hp. If he blows up on his own, the explosion deals more damage than before on your team, but deals barely any damage on his team. However, if you kill the enemy, he instantly explodes, doing a lot of damage to your enemies, and no damage at all to your team.

This is a Beat'Em Up, I should have a reason to get close and beat the enemies up, instead of sitting in a corner waiting for them to blow up.

There's some other areas I have a problem too, like 13- Taking Care Of The Family having questionable hurtboxes, and 14- An Offer You Can't Refuse, both having really annoying boss fights. 

- Defensive mechanics

There's 5. Counter, Dodge, Tech, Block and Parry. And I have a problem with most of them, also the tutorial doesn't explain that Tech and Dodge allows you to go into different lanes.

Counter is the worst. It needs a bigger hitbox, more damage, and multiple hits to properly deal with armored enemies.

Dodging is pretty much useless. It needs to allow the player to clip through enemies when you do it. 

Techs needs more I-frames.

Parry is way too powerful and works on most attacks, it freezes the enemy and makes them take +50% damage. It needs the damage boost removed.

- While I did praise the huge amount of moves the characters have, this is also a detriment. Alot of moves are weak or just useless, so you end up using just half of your character's moveset.

- Various youtubers and other famous people are playable. While this is cool, those people often do some stupid stuff in real life, which could taint the game if they do so.

[h2] Conclusion: [/h2]

This game is a 6/10, it's a good game, and I really like it, but it has a lot of flaws.

I'm gonna be honest, the first time I saw this game, I didn't buy it, it looked rough and more of a joke. Until I discovered that the people behind Streets of Rage 4 (a game I have over 300 hours on the PS4) also made this. So I bought it, and it did not disappoint.

It's wild to see Guard Crush Games start from making a silly game on Xbox 360, to releasing a better version on Steam, to doing the next Streets of Rage, and now Absolum.

Who would have thought that 10 years later they would be making better Beat'Em Ups, when they started from something so simple. They even updated the game 10 years after.      

Thanks Guard Crush, and good luck on whatever games you do next.

Streets of Fury EX is an unapologetically chaotic love letter to classic side-scrolling brawlers, one that embraces the raw energy of arcade-era beat ’em ups while boldly pushing the genre in a more technical, almost fighting-game-inspired direction. Developed and published by Guard Crush, the game immediately sets itself apart with its aggressive tone, exaggerated characters, and relentless pace, evoking memories of Streets of Rage and Final Fight while making it clear that it has no interest in being a simple nostalgia exercise. Instead, it aims to reimagine what a beat ’em up can feel like when depth and absurdity are given equal importance.

At the heart of the experience is a combat system that is far more intricate than it initially appears. While it’s easy to pick up and start throwing punches, kicks, and grabs, true mastery requires an understanding of cancels, air combos, dodges, and character-specific techniques. Combat flows quickly, encouraging constant movement and aggression, and rewards players who experiment rather than rely on repetitive attacks. The game borrows heavily from competitive fighting games in its approach to hit confirmation and combo chaining, which gives encounters a surprising level of nuance. As a result, battles feel less like chaotic crowd control and more like fast-paced skirmishes where positioning, timing, and awareness matter.

One of the game’s most striking features is its extensive roster of playable characters. With a large selection available, each fighter brings a distinct playstyle, move set, and rhythm to the action. Some characters excel at speed and aerial dominance, others rely on brute force or crowd control, and learning how each one operates dramatically changes how the game feels. This variety significantly enhances replayability, as replaying stages with different characters can feel like a completely new experience. The inclusion of unlockable content and alternate modes further encourages experimentation and long-term engagement.

The structure of Streets of Fury EX goes beyond a straightforward story mode, offering a collection of additional modes that add depth and longevity. Survival challenges push players to endure increasingly overwhelming waves of enemies, testing endurance and mechanical skill. Versus and challenge modes shift the focus toward competitive play and mastery, transforming the game into something closer to a hybrid brawler-fighter. There is also a light gang-building element in alternate modes that adds a playful layer of progression without overcomplicating the core experience. These modes help prevent repetition and ensure that the game remains engaging even after multiple playthroughs.

Visually, the game leans heavily into a gritty, digitized aesthetic that feels intentionally rough and unfiltered. Character sprites and animations have a low-fi, almost VHS-like quality that reinforces the game’s street-level brutality and arcade roots. While this visual style can be polarizing, it complements the game’s tone and frenetic action remarkably well. Environments are simple but functional, prioritizing clarity and flow over decorative detail, while animations effectively convey impact and momentum during combat. The audio design follows a similar philosophy, delivering punchy sound effects and energetic music that enhance the feeling of constant motion and intensity.

Streets of Fury EX truly shines in multiplayer, particularly in local cooperative play. Sharing the screen with friends amplifies the chaos and highlights the game’s strengths, turning every encounter into a noisy, frantic spectacle of flying bodies and overlapping combos. Cooperative play encourages coordination and experimentation, while competitive modes allow players to test their mastery of characters and mechanics against each other. The lack of online multiplayer does limit accessibility for some players, but the game’s design clearly prioritizes couch co-op and shared, immediate experiences over remote play.

Community reception over the years reflects a strong appreciation for the game’s depth, ambition, and unapologetic personality. Many players praise its willingness to challenge genre conventions and its surprisingly high skill ceiling, while others highlight the satisfaction of gradually mastering its systems. Criticism tends to focus on its visual roughness and the learning curve, which can be intimidating for those expecting a simpler, more traditional beat ’em up. However, for players willing to invest time and curiosity, these same qualities often become part of the game’s appeal.

Ultimately, Streets of Fury EX stands as a bold and distinctive entry in the modern beat ’em up landscape. It doesn’t aim for polish or mass appeal, but instead commits fully to delivering fast, technical, and wildly energetic combat that rewards dedication and experimentation. By blending arcade sensibilities with fighting-game mechanics and a strong sense of identity, it offers an experience that feels both familiar and refreshingly unconventional. For fans of brawlers who crave depth, intensity, and replayability, it remains a standout title that proves the genre still has room to evolve in exciting and unexpected ways.

Je suis descendu dans Streets of Fury EX comme Rimbaud dans l’Enfer de ses illuminations — ivre de bitume, tremblant sous les néons, frappé par l’éclair d’un beat’em up céleste !

Et là, dans le fracas des poings et le chaos du pixel — il est apparu.
BOB LENNON.
Ô Bob, Bob le Grand, Bob le Rouge, Bob le Feu —
Un ouragan en manteau de flamme, une tornade d’uppercuts surréalistes !
Son attaque spéciale est un cri de l’âme, une gifle cosmique à la morosité moderne.
Quand il frappe, c’est toute la francophonie qui vibre !
Quand il crie, les étoiles saignent du sang de la hype !

Et puis Jesse Pinkmen, l’évadé de la série, le dealer devenu guerrier —
Yo, ce gars-là distribue des baffes comme des sentences existentielles.
Chaque coup est un slam, chaque combo est une réplique : YEAH, SCIENCE, B**H !*
Il glisse sur le pavé comme une comète de rage, cassant des mâchoires dans une poésie du ghetto.
Sa technique ? Une élégance crade, une danse de rue habitée par le spectre du chaos.

Benzaï, noble esthète de l’étrange, vibre comme une onde punk dans cette symphonie de baffes.
Il combat comme il parle : trop fort, trop vrai, trop génial.
Sa moustache est une légende. Ses coups, une prière techno-anarchique.

Mais ce jeu, ce jeu mes amis...
C’est un poème musclé, une épiphanie beat’em up,
Une orgie de sprites, un trip d’arcade halluciné !
La rue y est un poème nerveux, un slam de violence pixelisée.
On n’y joue pas : on y entre en transe.

Les combos sont des strophes.
Les KO sont des alexandrins explosifs.
Le style ? Baroque, brutal, beau.

Et moi, pauvre joueur halluciné,
je vous le jure sur mon pad et mes doigts endoloris :
CE JEU EST UN MANIFESTE.
Et Bob Lennon est son prophète !

Poorly thought out meme game. Annoying lanes lock you into fighting only certain groups of enemies, and enemies are really bad about coming after you. They'd rather wait in whichever lane you're not in, grouping up such that they can strike you if you try to hop over to join them.

This beatemup has blocking for the obvious reason that enemy encounters are designed for mashing. Spacing and orientation are less of a priority than filling up the screen with enemies, many of whom can ignore hits of your attacks or strike outside your range. The first hit of enemy attacks stuns you, for which there's a "counter" button that forces enemies away. The result is a button-mashing experience where it doesn't feel like skill matters much. I personally find beatemups of this type, or that exist only to mash buttons, to be a boring waste of time.

The UI is trash. Specific coloring is used to illustrate some differences between unit types, but the same coloring could mean friend or enemy when applied to different enemies. This is really poor visual communication. In general, the photos feel less like a stylistic choice and more a lazy route as nothing really interesting is done with it. The photos, especially for the cameo characters, are here as a joke and the joke is lazy.

The specials and dashing are easy. That's about it.
